title: Growing Your Habits from Tiny to Transformative
coreMove: Let a tiny habit grow on its own terms by watching for the natural expansion signal, then either stretch the behavior, multiply it, or graft a new tiny habit onto the same anchor — without forcing the growth before the wiring is set.

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospice nurse who started with one deep breath before entering a patient's room and now wonders whether to add a second breath, a silent intention, or both
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader whose first tiny habit has stuck for three weeks and is itching to expand it
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether she preserves the calm the original habit gave her or accidentally turns it into a checklist that drains her again
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she notices she wants to expand because the behavior already feels easy, not because she is trying to push through resistance, and she chooses to stretch the existing breath rather than stack a new one

exampleSpecs.domain: a freight dispatcher who has been doing two squats after every coffee refill for a month and feels his body lean toward a third rep on its own
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who keeps wondering when 'tiny' stops being the rule
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether he honors the natural pull and lets the habit grow, or freezes at two squats because the book told him to stay tiny forever
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the moment of growth comes from the body initiating, not from a calendar reminder, and he simply lets the third squat happen without renegotiating the recipe

exampleSpecs.domain: two roommates, a bike mechanic and a community college instructor, comparing notes at the kitchen table about a flossing habit one of them grew too fast and abandoned
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who has already overshot one tiny habit and quietly given up
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the instructor can diagnose what went wrong without blaming herself, and try again with a smaller starter
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the mechanic names the specific failure as a design error — she scaled before celebration was automatic — and reframes restarting as engineering, not penance

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional bakery manager who started a tiny habit of writing one sentence in a notebook after locking the back door, and now finds three other anchors in her day calling out for their own tiny habits
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who has one habit working and is wondering whether to deepen it or branch
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether she multiplies habits responsibly across her day or spreads herself so thin that the original one collapses too
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she chooses one new anchor, leaves the others alone for now, and articulates the rule she is using: a new tiny habit only after the previous one stops needing attention

exampleSpecs.domain: a retired plumber teaching his grandson to practice violin, mapping his own habit-growth experience onto the kid's daily practice
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who teaches, parents, or coaches and wants to apply growth principles to someone else
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the grandson keeps loving the violin or starts dreading it because grandpa pushed the practice up from two minutes to twenty too quickly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the grandfather catches himself wanting to scale up because of his own pride, pulls back, and lets the boy choose when to play one more line

exampleSpecs.domain: a forty-six-year-old physical therapist reflecting on the difference between the tiny habits that grew quietly into part of who she is and the ones that stayed exactly tiny forever — and noticing she values both kinds
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who suspects 'transformative' means every habit must eventually become big
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether she releases the pressure to grow every habit and accepts that some tiny habits stay tiny and still count
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: she names a specific habit that has stayed at thirty seconds for two years and articulates why its smallness is the feature, not the failure
